contributions.headingText: Angiomatosis is a histologically benign vascular proliferation that affects a large segment of the breast.

Not recommended: diffuse angioma; giant vascular tumour.
In all cases, angiomatosis involves the interlobular stroma of the breast. The intralobular stroma is spared. Occasionally, the lesion may extend into the subcutaneous tissue and the skin.

Most patients present with painless, slow enlargement of the breast. Angiomatosis may form large palpable masses, ranging from 20 to 220 mm {4051097;3179956;31088938}. The lesion is usually entirely within the breast parenchyma. Massive enlargement during pregnancy has been reported {3179956}. One case showed a vertical manner of growth involving the breast parenchyma, subcutaneous tissue, and skin {26456034}. Overlying skin may show hyperpigmentation, faint blue discolouration, or papules {3179956;26456034}. The lesion may be transilluminated {3179956}. Imaging studies can be helpful in identifying the tumour as being vascular in nature, but are not helpful in differentiating a benign from a malignant tumour. Sonography shows multiple irregular anechoic spaces separated by thin septa. Moderate blood flow can be demonstrated with colour Doppler. MRI reveals a multiseptated cystic mass, with T2-weighted imaging showing hyperintense tubular structures {26456034;24965677;28491155}.

Angiomatosis is a very rare vascular lesion, with only a few case reports published {29479420;28491155}. It can be congenital or acquired. Cases have been described in patients from birth up to 59 years of age {4051097;26456034;28491155}, although most cases have been observed in young women (< 40 years old). Only 1 case in a male patient, a 7-year-old boy, has been reported {12632645}.

Angiomatosis presents as a cystic, red, spongy, extensive lesion simulating an angiosarcoma. The cystic spaces contain haemorrhagic or serosanguinous material {4051097;3179956}. One case showed a large, central, unilocular cystic space filled with serosanguinous fluid {3179956}.

In the usual pattern, the process consists of a proliferation of vascular channels with wide variation in calibre, diffusely growing throughout the breast parenchyma and showing some degree of anastomosis {4051097}. Vascular structures are uniformly distributed and surround the ducts and lobules. Invasion of the intralobular stroma is absent. The lesions are unencapsulated, with poorly defined infiltrative borders. The vessels are lined by flat inconspicuous endothelium without atypia or mitoses. They show sparse supporting mural tissue that is virtually free of smooth muscle. Blood vessels may contain erythrocytes in their lumina. Lymphatic vessels, empty or with aggregates of lymphocytes, can be present {4051097;1818036}. Occasional foci of capillary-sized vessels can be observed within the wall of large venous structures or in the vicinity {1497117;3444663}. A considerable part of the tumour is composed of breast parenchyma incorporated among the vascular structures {4051097}. The lesion may extend to the overlying skin {26456034} or to the underlying pectoralis muscle. If the lesion is observed on core biopsy, complete excision and examination are required for a definitive diagnosis. An uncommon pattern of angiomatosis shows capillary morphology and consists predominantly of collections of benign, small, capillary-sized vessels arranged in nodules, often showing a larger vessel in the centre. These structures are dispersed throughout the fibrous stroma and adipose tissue {1497117}.

Immunohistochemical testing for CD31 and podoplanin (recognized by D2-40) highlights the endothelial cells lining the vascular channels of the lesion {28049578;31088938}. Endothelial cell proliferation as measured by the Ki-67 proliferation index is low (< 2% in almost all cases) {28491155;31088938}.

A critical matter is the distinction from low-grade angiosarcoma, which can histologically show areas with a benign appearance. Unlike angiosarcoma, angiomatosis exhibits a uniform pattern of vessel distribution, and the endothelial nuclei are bland, without hyperchromasia. There are no papillae, endothelial tufting, blood lakes, or necrosis. Endothelial cell mitoses are rare or absent {28049578}. Dissection of vessels into lobules with disruption of the lobules is not observed {28676174}.

Diffuse dermal angiomatosis of the breast is a different disorder. It is a rare reactive angioproliferation in the skin, recognized as a distinct subtype of cutaneous reactive angioendotheliomatosis {26645009}.
Diagnosis of angiomatosis has not been made on cytopathology.

Essential: anastomosing vascular spaces of varying calibre; diffuse growth within breast parenchyma without invading lobules; regularly distributed, flat, inconspicuous endothelial cells lacking hyperchromasia.

Incompletely excised angiomatosis has a high risk of local recurrence, but metastasis and malignant transformation have not been described {3179956;28491155;29479420;31088938}. Complete surgical excision is commonly performed. In some cases, mastectomy may be necessary to control a bulky lesion, but whenever possible it is preferable not to perform such extensive surgery.
